full_judgment:
8. The plaintiff respondent's case in Title Suit No. 171 of 1985 is that, the property mentioned in the schedule 1 of the plaint originally belonged to three brothers, namely, Mahim Chandra Aich, Satish Chandra Aich and Opendra Chandra Aich who became owners of the same on the basis of a kabuliyat dated 31st Baishak, 1332 BS. Thereafter, by amicable partition between themselves Mahim Chandra Aich got the land mentioned in the schedule 1 of the plaint and was in exclusive possession of the property for more than 50 years by constructing building and huts thereon. Mahim Chandra Aich died leaving his only son, Binayendra Aich who was also in actual physical possession of the suit property for more than 12 years. He died leaving behind his wife Ava Rani Aich and two sons, namely, Dharanindra Aich and Bijoy Krishna Aich. Bijoy Krishna relinquished his claim in his paternal property. Thus Ava Rani Aich and Dharanindra Aich remained in possession of the suit property of late Binayendra Aich in assertion of their right, title and possession thereon. The record of right was finally published in the name of their heirs. They sold the suit land by registered kabala dated 31-1-1972 to the plaintiff-respondent No.1, ABM Hasan Kabir who went into possession of the first schedule property of the plaint along with other suit properties which was under possession of the defendant appellants as monthly tenants. The defendant appellants agreed to pay monthly rent to the plaintiff. Thereafter, on demand of the rent, the defendant appellants refused to pay rent and finally on 2-11-1981 denied the right, title and interest of the plaintiff in respect of the suit property. Hence, the Title Suit No. 171 of 1985 was initiated. 

 18. The defendant-appellants' claim that their landlord Hari Prasad Das's father Baroda Prasad Das took settlement from BinoyendraAich in 1940 and, as such, it cannot be said that the origin of their tenancy for residential purpose was unknown. But, in fact, they could not produce any paper in support of their claim. Further, they do not claim to have constructed any permanent structure on the land to the knowledge of Baroda Prasad Das, from whom they took the settlement. On the other hand, they claim that Baroda Prasad Das erected twelve huts in plot No. 947 and used to reside in some huts with his family and used to possess the other huts through monthly tenants. Upon these facts no substantial findings can be made out that any pucca building on the land was built to the knowledge of the landlord to justify the presumption of permanency of tenancy. The defendant-appellants also claim that the Municipal holding was also created in his father's name and he has been paying municipal taxes regularly. Admittedly, all the courts have found them in possession but they could not produce any patta kabuliyat in support of the alleged settlement in favour of Baroda Prasad Das from Binoyendra Aich in the year 1940. Three typed receipts have been marked as exhibit I series in Title Suit No. 133 of 1981 to prove the payment of ground taxes to Binayendra Aich. In these receipts it is mentioned that Rs. 60.00 was received by Binayendra Aich in respect of ground tax and municipal holding Nos. 185, 186 and 152(a) of Bazrapur Mohalla of Comilla Town. All the courts below held that from these receipts it could not be said that Baroda Prasad took settlement of the said land from Binayendra Aich. We do not also find any reason to disagree with them. Thus the defendant appellants failed to establish uniform payment of rent raising difficulties in the way of presumption of permanency of tenancy. 

 20. Lastly, Mr Khandkar Mahbubuddin, has relied on 29 CWN 138, 128 and 43 CWN 828 to show that if a person is in possession of a land for a very long time, there is a presumption in his favour under section 110 of the Evidence Act. There is no dispute as to the proposition of law. But we are to see whether the facts upon which reliance has been placed unequivocally point to long possession by the defendant appellants of the suit property. The presumption under section 110 in this case would apply only if two conditions are satisfied viz, that the possession of the person claiming long possession is not prima facie wrongful and secondly, the title of the person, in this case the plaintiff-respondent, against whom the long possession is claimed is not proved. The courts below found that the defendant-appellants are in possession but they could not prove their title or that they are not in possession to the knowledge of the real owner upon denying his title or any kabuliyat or deed of settlement. On the other hand, the plaintiff-respondent has proved their title by registered kabala executed on 13-11-1978 for valuable consideration. This kabala has not been disbelieved by the courts below. This hits at the root of the claim by the defendant- appellants on the suit land on the basis of long possession since their claim of title of the suit property has been disbelieved by the courts below. No doubt the defendant-appellants' possession for a long time and by succession are material. But the claim of long possession remains precarious because of the finding of title of the suit land in favour of the plaintiff- respondent by courts below.
